segments.title: Why warships cannot be future-proofed against unknown threats
segments.summary: The Cressys illustrate why an expensive, long-lived warship can be designed sensibly yet still encounter technologies its creators could not reasonably anticipate.
segments.body: Dr. Clarke uses the Cressy class to distinguish prudent design margins from hindsight masquerading as foresight. Retrofitting torpedo protection could mean adding speed-reducing bulges or rebuilding the ship's interior so extensively that a new hull would be more economical. The problem was especially severe between HMS Warrior and the First World War, when armor, engines, propellers, guns, ammunition, and fire control passed through several technological generations. A ship conceived in the 1890s could therefore remain serviceable while becoming poorly matched to a threat that barely existed when its requirements were written. This watch point frames the rest of the class history as a lesson in design uncertainty rather than a simple story of bad ships.

evidence.note: The passage connects future-proofing to the cost of rebuilding old cruisers and surveys rapid changes in armor, propulsion, weapons, ammunition, and fire control before 1914.

segments.title: Cressy at the turn from Victorian to modern cruisers
segments.summary: The Cressy class is placed between late Victorian armoured cruisers and the faster-changing cruiser designs of the twentieth century.
segments.body: Dr. Clarke presents the class as both the end of a nineteenth-century design lineage and a starting point for later British armoured cruisers. Their requirements were being considered years before the first hulls were laid down, so they embodied assumptions from the mid-1890s rather than the world of 1914. William White's methodical process reduced the risk of adopting unsound ideas, but it also meant that concepts still being studied could only appear in later generations. The class was therefore credible for the tasks its designers understood while occupying an unforgiving point in a period of unusually rapid technological change. Its later fate should be read against that design chronology rather than treated as proof that the ships never had value.

evidence.note: The transcript calls the Cressys the last nineteenth-century cruisers and a starting point for twentieth-century cruiser development, then explains White's deliberate design process.

segments.title: Why the Royal Navy wanted the Cressy class
segments.summary: White's requirements combine fleet support, detached commerce protection, long coal endurance, and enough fighting power to meet foreign first-class cruisers.
segments.body: The ships were intended to reinforce battleships in close action, protect communications on detached service, and remain competitive with foreign first-class cruisers. Their full coal allowance of about 1,600 tons was intended to support roughly thirty days at ten knots or 120 hours at high sustained speed, revealing how endurance shaped a worldwide cruiser. Dr. Clarke distinguishes the advertised 21.5-knot top speed from the lower 19.75 knots that machinery and fuel could sustain over time. Normal displacement assumed only 800 tons of coal, so the requirement joined global range to practical loading limits. The Cressys were therefore neither small battleships nor simple commerce patrol vessels, but multi-role ships designed to connect fleet support with Britain's shipping and communications network.

evidence.note: White's design statement lists fleet, detached-service, commerce-protection, speed, and coal-endurance requirements.

segments.title: Coal endurance depended on fuel and shipboard expertise
segments.summary: Nominal bunker capacity was only the starting point because coal quality, improvised stowage, and trusted shipboard specialists shaped a cruiser's real range.
segments.body: Dr. Clarke pauses over the nominal 2,400-nautical-mile high-speed range to show why paper endurance was not the whole story. Better Welsh coal could reduce consumption, and some captains found extra spaces for fuel beyond the stated bunker capacity. He presents that improvisation as a command-team problem in which a captain relied on an experienced chief or other non-commissioned specialist to make the ship's endurance requirement work in practice. Such personnel networks were not new to steam navies; capable captains had long carried trusted junior officers and non-commissioned problem-solvers between appointments. The watch point connects coal figures, shipboard expertise, and the human organization behind global cruiser operations.

evidence.note: The passage converts the high-speed endurance figure, discusses Welsh coal and extra stowage, and connects practical problem-solving to trusted chiefs, NCOs, and junior officers.

segments.title: Cressy machinery, protection, and cost
segments.summary: The class's displacement, machinery, armour scheme, weapons, and price establish what a large late-1890s British armoured cruiser actually represented.
segments.body: Dr. Clarke gives the class's baseline as roughly 12,000 tons, thirty Belleville boilers, and two triple-expansion engines driving twin shafts. The machinery was rated at 21,000 indicated horsepower for a designed top speed of about twenty-one knots, while an individual ship cost roughly £725,760. Protection ranged from a two-to-six-inch belt and one-to-three-inch deck to six-inch barbettes and turrets, a twelve-inch conning tower, and five-inch bulkheads. Two submerged eighteen-inch torpedo tubes supplemented the two 9.2-inch guns, twelve six-inch guns, and lighter quick-firing weapons. These numbers provide the technical baseline for understanding why the Cressys were powerful first-class cruisers by late-1890s standards but not compact battleships.

evidence.note: The transcript lists displacement, Belleville boilers, triple-expansion machinery, horsepower, speed, cost, armament, torpedo tubes, and armour thicknesses.

segments.title: How armoured cruisers could reinforce a battle line
segments.summary: The fleet-adjunct requirement envisioned armoured cruisers adding hulls, gunfire, and torpedoes when an enemy also committed cruisers beside its battleships.
segments.body: White's phrase “adjuncts to battleships” meant more than escort duty. British planners expected foreign fleets to bring cruisers into a battle line, where extra quick-firing guns and a lucky hit could alter an apparently even contest. Armoured cruisers therefore gave the Royal Navy a way to add hulls, heavy gunfire, and torpedoes beside its battleships. Dr. Clarke illustrates the concept with two mixed lines double-enveloping six enemy battleships and forcing the central ships to fight on both beams. The example explains why the Cressys' broadside and torpedoes were designed for fleet action even though their independent cruising role is often more familiar.

evidence.note: The transcript explains how armoured cruisers could support a battleship line, add numbers and torpedoes, and help double-envelop an opposing force.

segments.title: Overwhelming force in Victorian naval coercion
segments.summary: The Cressys' fleet-adjunct role belonged to a strategic culture that sought decisive superiority rather than a carefully calibrated military response.
segments.body: Dr. Clarke contrasts modern language about proportional response with a nineteenth-century preference for making resistance impossible. A hostile squadron might be double-enveloped, destroyed, and followed by a blockade or bombardment of its principal harbor. Cruisers that could fight alongside battleships helped create that numerical and tactical overmatch. The point was not merely to punish an opponent but to remove its immediate ability to repeat the challenge. This passage gives the Cressys' heavy armament and fleet role a wider political context: they were instruments of coercion as well as combatants.

evidence.note: The passage contrasts proportional response with a nineteenth-century pattern of destroying a squadron and then blockading or bombarding its harbor.

segments.title: Cressy armament and the cost of low casemates
segments.summary: The class carried a formidable 9.2-inch and six-inch battery, but much of its broadside could be masked by heavy seas.
segments.body: The Cressys concentrated their strength on the broadside, with a pair of 9.2-inch guns backed by twelve six-inch weapons and a large quick-firing battery. Four of the six six-inch guns on each side sat low enough to become difficult to use in rough water. That limitation reflected expectations of Channel and Mediterranean service rather than the harsher South Atlantic or high-latitude seas. The 9.2-inch shell weighed nearly four times as much as the standard six-inch shell, giving the ship a slower-firing but much harder-hitting weapon for an armored opponent. The arrangement explains both why the class looked formidable on paper and why weather could sharply reduce its practical broadside.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the broadside arrangement, low casemates in heavy seas, and the shell-weight difference between the six-inch and 9.2-inch guns.

segments.title: How the Admiralty enforced class standardization
segments.summary: Different private yards built the class, but Admiralty officials enforced common boilers, machinery standards, and internal arrangements.
segments.body: Dr. Clarke contrasts British construction control with the greater variation found in some contemporary foreign classes. France's land threats and the priority given to its army made naval authority less concentrated, whereas several British private yards and machinery firms could be held to one Admiralty pattern. The Cressys therefore used common boiler types, performance standards, and internal arrangements despite being built by different contractors. The Director of Naval Construction, Third Sea Lord, and senior engineering authority all had to approve the completed ship before the builder was paid. A yard that departed from the accepted pattern also risked losing later naval work to competitors or to the royal dockyards. Because these firms invested in naval technology and depended on major orders, the threat of withholding a contract carried real financial force. Standardisation was enforced through concentrated technical authority and purchasing power, not merely through drawings sent to contractors.

evidence.note: The transcript explains common machinery requirements, official sign-off, payment leverage, and the threat of withholding later naval contracts.

segments.title: HMS Cressy from China Station to Heligoland Bight
segments.summary: Cressy's station work, long reserve period, and support after Heligoland Bight show a useful cruiser with relatively little wear before her 1914 loss.
segments.body: Cressy entered Fleet Reserve in May 1901 and then commissioned for the China Station, although a steering failure delayed her departure. She reached Colombo and Singapore that November, completed a full overseas tour, and later served on the North America and West Indies Station before returning to reserve in 1909. When war began she was less than fifteen years old and had spent only four or five years in commission, which undercuts the image of a worn-out ship sent out as expendable bait. Cressy joined the Seventh Cruiser Squadron and did not fire at Heligoland Bight, but the squadron's approach helped persuade the German force to withdraw. She then carried 165 unwounded German survivors recovered after the battle back to the Nore under Bacchante's escort. Her career before 22 September 1914 combined imperial presence, reserve readiness, and practical support to the Harwich Force.

evidence.note: The transcript follows Cressy through China and West Indies service, reserve, the Seventh Cruiser Squadron, Heligoland Bight, and the transport of German survivors.

segments.title: HMS Sutlej's escort, training, and convoy career
segments.summary: Sutlej moved from battleship escort and China service to training, convoy protection, and depot work across a varied twenty-year career.
segments.body: Sutlej's name leads into a brief account of the hard-fought First Anglo-Sikh War between the Sikh state and the East India Company in Punjab. Her hull was begun by a Clydebank predecessor that John Brown and Company later absorbed as the armour, railway, and heavy-engineering firm entered shipbuilding. Commissioned in 1902, Sutlej attended Edward VII's coronation fleet review, exercised in the Aegean, and escorted the damaged battleship HMS Hood from Gibraltar to Chatham after Aboukir covered the earlier leg from Malta. She then served on the China Station and became a boys' training ship on the North America and West Indies Station, where sailors could gain real overseas experience at comparatively low risk of war. A boiler explosion killed four men during 1910 manoeuvres, but the cruiser returned for First World War convoy duties off Liberia, Ireland, and the Azores. She finished as an accommodation and depot ship before being sold in 1921, a career far broader than the class's most famous disaster.

evidence.note: The passage covers the First Anglo-Sikh War name context, John Brown's yard acquisition, Hood escort, China and training service, a fatal boiler explosion, convoy work, and depot service.

segments.title: Aboukir's exercises as a signal of support for Greece
segments.summary: Combined maneuvers and sailor landings in Greek waters let the Royal Navy communicate political support without issuing an overt threat.
segments.body: Aboukir joined Channel and Mediterranean ships for exercises in Greek waters in 1902. The landing of naval personnel was formally an exercise, but its location and scale carried a message to Russia and the Ottoman Empire. Britain could demonstrate interest in the survival of the Greek state while preserving diplomatic deniability about the purpose of the activity. A first-class cruiser was useful in this setting because its visible military power made the signal legible without requiring combat. The episode is a compact example of naval presence operating as diplomacy.

evidence.note: The transcript describes combined maneuvers and sailor landings in Greek waters as a deliberate signal of British support for Greece.

segments.title: HMS Hogue's service and Heligoland support
segments.summary: Hogue's overseas, training, reserve, and towing work culminated in practical support to Tyrwhitt's damaged flagship after Heligoland Bight.
segments.body: Hogue was named for the Battle of La Hogue in the Nine Years' War and was built by Vickers, Sons and Maxim at Barrow. After commissioning in 1902 she served with the Channel Squadron, collided with the merchant ship Marouf in 1904, and then transferred to the China Station. She later became a boys' training ship on the North America and West Indies Station, entered reserve, and suffered a coal-bunker explosion that killed two men before a lengthy 1912–1913 refit. Mobilised with the Seventh Cruiser Squadron in August 1914, Hogue arrived after the fighting at Heligoland Bight but towed Commodore Reginald Tyrwhitt's damaged light cruiser Arethusa back to port. Dr. Clarke stresses that the approaching armoured cruisers were part of the support that encouraged the German withdrawal. He also notes how differently the class might be remembered had it arrived soon enough to engage an already weakened enemy in the battle for which its guns had been designed.

evidence.note: The transcript covers Hogue's name, building and station career, fatal bunker explosion, refit, and tow of Tyrwhitt's Arethusa after Heligoland Bight.

segments.title: The torpedo threat the Cressys were built to defeat
segments.summary: The class did carry defenses against torpedo attack, but its quick-firing guns were intended to stop surface torpedo boats rather than submerged submarines.
segments.body: Dr. Clarke argues that the Cressys were designed against the torpedo threat visible to naval architects in the late 1890s. Their numerous twelve-pounders were intended to destroy attacking torpedo boats before those craft reached an effective firing position. Submarines existed only in tiny numbers and had not yet demonstrated the operational threat seen in 1914. The ships were therefore not devoid of torpedo defense; they were equipped for the wrong delivery platform from the perspective of later experience. This distinction shows how a sound response to an identified threat can still fail when the means of attack changes.

evidence.note: The passage says the quick-firing battery was meant to stop torpedo boats and contrasts that understood threat with the still-novel submarine.

segments.title: Why Britain treated the German Navy as an exceptional threat
segments.summary: British deployment choices reflected a professional respect for German naval competence that Dr. Clarke compares with the Royal Navy's older view of the Dutch.
segments.body: The Cressys' wartime employment cannot be separated from how British officers assessed their opponents. Dr. Clarke argues that the German Navy was considered more capable than the French fleet and inherited the place once occupied by the Dutch as Britain's most respected maritime rival. That estimate made German moves seem especially dangerous even when the Royal Navy enjoyed greater overall strength. It also encouraged Britain to retain useful hulls near the North Sea rather than dispersing every older cruiser to distant stations. The passage shows how perceptions of enemy quality shape force allocation as much as raw ship counts do.

evidence.note: The transcript says Britain considered the German Navy highly capable and compares its perceived quality with the earlier Royal Navy view of the Dutch.

segments.title: Bacchante's officers and the wartime command bottleneck
segments.summary: Douglas Gamble's staff aboard Bacchante illustrates both the Royal Navy's officer-development networks and the scarcity of independent fleet commands in the North Sea war.
segments.body: Bacchante served as Rear Admiral Douglas Gamble's flagship with Reginald Tyrwhitt as flag captain and Bertram Ramsay as flag lieutenant. Dr. Clarke treats the quality of those appointments as evidence that Gamble was trusted to train and advance talented officers. The First World War nevertheless concentrated the main naval contest in a small number of senior North Sea commands. Keeping Jellicoe in place was operationally sensible, but it limited the independent fleets available to other capable admirals. Gamble's later career therefore opens a broader discussion of how command structure can constrain promotion even in a navy rich in talent.

evidence.note: The passage identifies Gamble, Tyrwhitt, and Ramsay, then explains how the concentration of wartime fleet command restricted opportunities for other senior officers.

segments.title: Bacchante's gunfire support at Gallipoli
segments.summary: Bacchante repeatedly manoeuvred for effective fire at Gallipoli, suppressed Ottoman artillery, and supported the Anzac battles before later convoy service.
segments.body: After the loss of three sisters, Bacchante and Euryalus escorted shipping between England and Gibraltar and then moved to Egypt. Bacchante arrived too late for the Ottoman raid on the Suez Canal but soon joined the Gallipoli campaign. She manoeuvred bow-on toward the shore and repeatedly adjusted position to improve her fire against Ottoman guns. At Anzac Cove she joined three pre-dreadnoughts in suppressing Turkish artillery during the major attack of 19 May, then later bombarded troops around Lone Pine and Chunuk Bair. Captain Algernon Boyle was ashore commanding the Anzac evacuation even though Bacchante herself was absent. The cruiser remained in the Mediterranean, collided with the armoured cruiser Achilles in 1917, and finished the war as flagship of the Ninth Cruiser Squadron at Sierra Leone. Her career shows the continuing value of endurance and heavy gunfire in amphibious support and convoy work.

evidence.note: The transcript describes Bacchante's convoy transfer, Gallipoli manoeuvring and gunfire, the Anzac battles and evacuation, and later Sierra Leone service.

segments.title: Fire and dockyard accidents delayed Euryalus
segments.summary: A major dock fire and further accidents forced several yards and the Royal Navy to reconstruct Euryalus before she could enter service two years behind her sisters.
segments.body: Euryalus was lying beside Ramsden Dock when a major fire spread from the wharf to the newly launched cruiser. She was badly damaged before being hauled clear and then had to be towed to Cammell Laird for repair. The ship subsequently slipped from her blocks in dry dock and collided with an auxiliary vessel during trials. Vickers, Cammell Laird, and Devonport all contributed to recovering the project. Her delayed completion in January 1904 shows both the vulnerability of a capital-intensive shipbuilding program to yard accidents and the industrial coordination needed to rescue a damaged hull.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the Ramsden Dock fire, dry-dock slip, trials collision, repair at Cammell Laird and Devonport, and completion two years after her sisters.

segments.title: Euryalus from fleet flagship to Gallipoli and the Red Sea
segments.summary: Euryalus served as a station flagship, training ship, Southern Force flagship, landing transport, gunfire ship, and unfinished minelayer.
segments.body: After her delayed completion, Euryalus became flagship on the Australia Station and later a boys' training ship on the North America and West Indies Station. In August 1914 she flew Rear Admiral Arthur Christian's flag as the Southern Force guarded the eastern end of the English Channel. Her return to port for coal on 20 September left Aboukir, Hogue, and Cressy on patrol two days before their loss, after which Christian was relieved of command. At Cape Helles, Euryalus carried three companies of Lancashire Fusiliers and men of the Royal Naval Division toward W Beach and provided fire support for the landing. She later reinforced Egypt, refitted at Bombay, and bombarded barracks at Hodeida with Royal Indian Marine support. Four six-inch and four twelve-pounder guns were removed before she went to Hong Kong for conversion as a minelayer, but the work was unfinished when the war ended. The ship returned home in 1919 and was ultimately broken up in Germany, an ironic end to a cruiser with service across several imperial stations.

evidence.note: The passage covers Euryalus's station and training roles, Southern Force flag service, Cape Helles landings, Egypt and Red Sea operations, disarmament, and unfinished minelayer conversion.

segments.title: Admiralty micromanagement on the Broad Fourteens
segments.summary: Central orders kept the cruisers covering troop movements after weather removed their destroyers, leaving the local commander to execute a risky patrol configuration he had not chosen.
segments.body: The Southern Force was a combined formation built around Euryalus, the five Cressy-class cruisers, light cruisers, two destroyer flotillas, and ten submarines rather than an isolated “live bait” squadron. July war orders still governed the patrol in September, placing the force across routes near German bases while British troops moved to France. Dr. Clarke argues that early-war Admiralty micromanagement narrowed Rear Admiral Arthur Christian's discretion as heavy weather forced the destroyer flotillas apart and prevented the combined patrol from reforming. Christian could reposition his cruisers only within central instructions and then had to return Euryalus to refuel, leaving Captain J. E. Drummond in command of Aboukir, Hogue, and Cressy. Their screen was absent because it could not operate in the same conditions, not because the force had been designed to patrol without escorts. The sequence shifts attention from a simplistic claim of local incompetence to the interaction of command, weather, coal, troop protection, and an unfamiliar threat.

evidence.note: The passage sets out the combined Southern Force, war orders, Admiralty control, weather separation, Euryalus's need to refuel, and Christian's compliance before Drummond took charge.

segments.title: How U-9 sank Aboukir, Hogue, and Cressy
segments.summary: U-9 exploited short firing ranges and the cruisers' rescue response after officers initially interpreted Aboukir's explosion as a mine strike.
segments.body: In the war's first six weeks, Germany had sent out only ten submarines, lost two, and sunk no ships, so the threat looked operationally unproven. At 06:00 on 22 September, the three cruisers were patrolling at ten knots in line abreast, roughly two nautical miles apart, with periscope lookouts posted and guns crewed. Kapitänleutnant Otto Weddigen's U-9 surfaced after sheltering from the storm, sighted the formation, and hit Aboukir from about 550 yards. Because no submarine was seen, Captain Drummond assumed a mine strike and ordered Hogue and Cressy to close for rescue. U-9 then hit Hogue from roughly 300 yards, briefly exposed its bow under gunfire, and attacked Cressy after she tried to ram and then turned back toward survivors. The short ranges, failed steam-powered lifeboat winches, and instinct to help men in the water show how familiar rescue practice and limited information compounded the effect of a new weapon.

evidence.note: The transcript gives the early U-boat record, cruiser formation, Weddigen's successive short-range attacks, the mine assumption, rescue manoeuvres, lifeboat failure, and Cressy's attempted ram.

segments.title: Civilian rescue and the anti-submarine gap after U-9
segments.summary: Dutch steamships and sailing trawlers saved hundreds of sailors, while U-9 escaped a destroyer search conducted without mature anti-submarine weapons.
segments.body: Nearby sailing trawlers initially hesitated because the cruisers were believed to be in a minefield. The Dutch steamship Flora nevertheless approached and rescued 286 men, while Titan and two large sailing trawlers recovered many more. British destroyers did not reach the scene until 10:45, by which time civilian mariners had accepted much of the immediate danger. In total 837 men survived, but 62 officers and 1,397 ratings were killed. U-9 conserved its limited submerged electrical power by remaining underwater through the night and returning to base the next day. The pursuing destroyers had neither depth charges nor ASDIC, so the passage links civilian courage to the Royal Navy's still-immature ability to find and attack a submerged boat.

evidence.note: The transcript names Flora, Titan, the sailing trawlers, the destroyers' arrival, the casualty totals, U-9's submerged escape, and the lack of depth charges or ASDIC.

segments.title: The Cressy disaster, hindsight, and the escort lesson
segments.summary: The disaster exposed an escort and force-structure problem, but it did not prove that an 1890s cruiser should have been designed around an unproven submarine threat.
segments.body: Dr. Clarke argues that judging the ships solely by a submarine threat barely imaginable when they were designed turns hindsight into a false requirement. The Admiralty could reasonably have withdrawn the cruisers whenever weather removed their destroyer screen, but that lesson became clear only after operational experience exposed the danger. Blaming Arthur Christian also obscures the fact that he followed central orders, challenged them where he could, and left an experienced captain in command. Better subdivision or internal torpedo protection might have improved survival, but two very short-range hits could overwhelm far newer protective schemes as well. The immediate requirement was a destroyer escort able to deter or attack submarines. The wider fleet lesson is that a simple high-low mix of battlecruisers and light cruisers left too little modern capacity in the medium tier for demanding but non-capital-ship missions.

evidence.note: The transcript rejects anachronistic submarine-proofing expectations, defends Christian's compliance, weighs added protection, and argues for destroyer escorts plus a stronger medium tier.

segments.title: Why a Cressy would not have solved Coronel
segments.summary: Low casemate guns and limited practical speed made Cressy the wrong reinforcement for Cradock, unlike the later medium armoured cruisers Britain had stopped building.
segments.body: Dr. Clarke rejects the common suggestion that sending Cressy-class ships to Christopher Cradock would have fixed the British position at Coronel. Their low six-inch casemates would have been badly restricted in the rough sea, and their practical sustained speed of about 19.75 knots was below the advertised figure. HMS Defence, which Cradock had been promised, combined four 9.2-inch guns with a substantial 7.5-inch battery in a much more suitable twentieth-century design. The Duke of Edinburgh, Warrior, and Minotaur classes represent the medium armoured cruisers that could have changed the tactical balance. Continuing to order such ships might also have retired older Cressys before the war. Coronel therefore becomes a force-structure lesson: numbers alone were not enough when the available cruisers had the wrong speed, gun layout, and generation of design.

evidence.note: The transcript explains Cressy's low-gun and speed limits at Coronel, contrasts HMS Defence and later armoured-cruiser classes, and argues for continued medium-cruiser production.

segments.title: The unbuilt post-Minotaur medium-cruiser question
segments.summary: The closing design exercise asks what a continuing British medium armoured-cruiser line might have produced alongside the dreadnought fleet.
segments.body: Dr. Clarke closes the historical discussion by asking viewers to imagine the Royal Navy continuing low-rate armoured-cruiser production after the Minotaur class. The hypothetical ships would be built alongside post-Dreadnought battleships such as the Queen Elizabeth class and replace older nineteenth-century cruisers. He asks what form the next classes might have taken and whether annual batches of three or four, or the larger six-to-eight batches he preferred, would sustain the missing medium tier. The transcript poses rather than answers that question, so this watch point preserves it as a counterfactual design exercise instead of a factual procurement programme. It extends the video's force-structure argument by inviting the reader to translate an identified capability gap into a plausible prewar ship-design lineage.

evidence.note: The transcript asks viewers to design a continued post-Minotaur armoured-cruiser line built alongside later dreadnought classes and to consider likely batch sizes.
